CausalChain: DDR gene mutations -> Accumulation of DNA damage -> Elevated TMB and neoantigen load -> Activation of stress response mediators (e.g., ATM/ATR signaling) -> Upregulation of TGF-β signaling (with concomitant IFN-γ interplay) -> Enhanced PD-L1 expression and recruitment of immunosuppressive cells -> Establishment of an immune 'cold' tumor microenvironment -> Reduced efficacy of ICIs
Hypothesis: In BTCs harboring DDR gene alterations, the ensuing accumulation of DNA damage not only increases TMB and neoantigen load but also activates intrinsic stress response mediators that upregulate TGF‐β signaling. This upregulation, acting in concert with IFN‐γ, drives a compensatory increase in PD-L1 expression and the recruitment of immunosuppressive cell populations, culminating in an immune ‘cold’ tumor microenvironment that renders ICIs less effective. We hypothesize that dual therapeutic inhibition of TGF‐β and PD-L1 will restore immunogenicity and improve clinical responses in this BTC subset. Our approach utilizes state-of-the-art CRISPR-based models to manipulate DDR gene status, multi-omics analyses to delineate the molecular cascades, and sophisticated in vivo imaging to monitor tumor-immune interactions, thereby providing a precise experimental framework and patient stratification biomarkers.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTC) exhibiting DNA damage repair (DDR) gene alterations present a complex interplay between immune activation and suppression. In these tumors, DDR defects lead to the accumulation of DNA damage that elevates tumor mutational burden (TMB) and neoantigen presentation. However, this initial immune stimulation is counterbalanced by a stress‐induced activation of compensatory immunoregulatory pathways. We propose that DNA damage triggers intrinsic stress response mediators (e.g., through ATM/ATR signaling) that directly elevate TGF‐β production. TGF‐β, in synergy with IFN‐γ, then upregulates PD-L1 expression and promotes the recruitment of immunosuppressive cell populations, ultimately establishing an “immune cold” tumor microenvironment that undermines immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) efficacy. Leveraging advanced CRISPR-based genetic models, comprehensive multi-omics analyses, and high-resolution in vivo imaging, our study aims to dissect this cascade and to validate a combinatorial therapeutic strategy targeting both TGF‐β and PD-L1. This integrated approach not only refines the mechanistic understanding of DDR-induced immune modulation in BTC but also provides a translational roadmap for overcoming immunotherapeutic resistance.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis linked DDR alterations in BTC to increased TMB and neoantigen load, leading to compensatory TGF-β signaling and PD-L1 upregulation, which created an immune cold tumor microenvironment that reduces ICI efficacy. The revised hypothesis retains this core causal chain while explicitly incorporating stress response mediators (e.g., ATM/ATR signaling) as the mechanistic bridge between accumulated DNA damage and TGF‐β activation. It further clarifies the synergistic interplay between TGF‐β and IFN‐γ in upregulating PD-L1 and recruiting immunosuppressive cells. Moreover, the new version emphasizes the use of modern technological platforms (CRISPR, multi-omics, in vivo imaging) to empirically validate each step of the causal chain and to guide a dual-target therapeutic strategy, thereby enhancing both the novelty and practical implementability of the hypothesis.
